We have conversed with many gentlemen in prominent political positions: but to Abraham Lincoln must we accord the palm of frankness. He had no disguises. The subject of Southern slavery was touched upon, and Mr. Lincoln emphatically declared that it was his principle not to touch it where it exists, but to prevent its spread into Territories now free. He spoke of slavery as an institution that did not meet the universal sanction of the Southern people. "Public opinion is not always private opinion," he said, and instancing Lamartine's account of the execution of Louis XVI, wherein it appeared that, although the leading revolutionists were publicly obliged to declare in favor of that deed, they were privately opposed to it. He said that it was the same with many people in the South; they were obliged to sustain slavery, although they secretly abhorred the institution. He would protect the South in its institutions as they exist, and said that Southerners did not comprehend the position of the Republicans in regard to slavery. The Southern mind, he said, was laboring under the delusion that the Republicans were to liberate the slaves, who were to apply firebrands to the fields and dwellings of their masters, massacre old and young, and produce a state of anarchy and bloodshed in the South. He swept this assumption away by a decisive denial of correctness. He said he should like to go South and talk to the Southerners on this topic, were it not that the minds of some were so inflamed against him that they would not listen to his reasoning, but, on the other hand, might be inclined to inflict lynch law upon his person should he appear among them.

The conversation was lively, and occasionally interspersed with some brilliant flashes of wit and good nature from the Kentucky lady, his wife.

HIS PERSONAL APPEARANCE.

Mr. Lincoln's personal appearance has so often been described in the newspaper prints that it is unnecessary for me to enlarge upon it here; but as a great deal has been said about his ugliness, I will say a word or two on that score, if only for the purpose of enticing the attention of the ladies North and South. Men of the West may care for personal beauty in a woman, but in a man beauty constitutes a very small claim upon their regard. But Lincoln is not an ugly man. We are aware that almost every Representative goes up to the capital with a budget of local wants and local suggestions in his pocket. But they do not differ much from the people in customs of other countries. Still we do not see the applicability of the suggestions of the theory advanced by our contemporary, that the Ministerial Budget should or does serve no other purpose than an index of the Finance Committee of the Representatives.

That the private budgets serve, as says our contemporary, to express the wants of the country. These wants are expressed without a knowledge of what may be asked by others, and how far the revenues of the country will suffice to meet all their little demands: and we will frankly add that many of the motions and petitions in the house do not very clearly indicate that the movers or petitioners know exactly what they want. But when it is further added by our contemporary that the ministerial budget is like an expression of the wants of the country, we would certainly assent to the journalist that it should be so; but deny that it is in the present budget the expression of any want except of those who modestly ask for more when the public were thinking of asking them to take less. Our neighbor's sentence is as follows: "Both the one (the Representatives' little budget) and the other (the Monster Budget) are simple expressions of the wants of the public."

This is the question which we have undertaken to discuss in our two last issues: whether the report of the Minister of Finance is an expression of the wants of the public. We have submitted to our readers the proposition that, in the present condition of our finances, it is the Minister's duty to propose retrenchment and reform to see with quick apprehension where sinecures can be topped off, the number of unnecessary employees reduced without injury to the public service, the amount of salaries reduced without incurring the risk of compelling trustworthy men to retire and being obliged to supply their places with persons less competent and less trustworthy; and still further, it is his duty to point out wherever a judicious aperture may be in managing the economy. He has not done so; and in pursuance with what we deem our duty, we shall proceed to do in an imperfect way, as far as present space and time will allow us, that work which the paid servant of the public has left undone. Public salaries must be paid by taxes on the people imposed in one form and another, and therefore it is the legitimate sphere of this Journal to discuss them. If he whose duty it is to suggest reforms fails to do so, if the public receipts threaten loss, it is natural and reasonable to demand a like decrease in expenses. It is always an ungrateful task to suggest the reduction of salaries, or the dismissal of unnecessary employees, since the recipients look upon their salaries as vested rights; we therefore forbear to place the ministerial salaries at $1,000 per annum—more especially in view of the prominent fact that they themselves, being the best judges, say their services are worth double that. If they solicited the increase, it would be well to test the idea thoroughly, and perhaps a decrease may be arrived at. If not in their salaries, in the expenses of their offices and departments. Does not this nation bear the appearance of a small boy with his father's clothes on? Have we not too many offices? Cannot some of them be dispensed with? And are we not so situated as to make it advisable to look after such things? To care carefully to the outstanding of the public revenues—that they may be distributed not for the purpose of enriching any, but for the profit of all?

Taking for granted that these propositions are conceded to be indisputably true, it will be asked, what is the necessity of the expenditure of $500 per year to a Commissioner in London? What interests have we in that capital, which are more momentous than at Washington or at any other? Let it not be said to be a small sum so long as the Treasury is obliged to borrow money to pay it, or so long as it might be of benefit in instructing one rod of road or be employed in any way in aiding steam navigation among the islands. Does the presence of a Commissioner there, and the payment to him of this paltry sum, make us any more respectable in the eyes of the world or of the British Empire? Then let us use this sum, and let it be set apart for the payment of consular agents, for our own domestic convenience, trusting in the fact that if our consuls should, in the course of time, have any work to do, their fees will suffice for their remuneration, and resting assured, that if they have no work to do, and therefore get no pay, no injustice will be done to them.

SIR: In looking over your political Textbook, I find an important error in your statement of the facts concerning the Baltimore Convention in relation to the admission of the delegates from Georgia. You substance that one half the original delegates or those who seceded from one half of the contingent delegation under the lead of Hon. Herschel V. Johnson, Hon. James Gardiner of the Union Constitutionalists, and Mr. Johnson, chairman, were admitted by the Convention at Baltimore. There is no error therein.

The mistake is, the Committee on Credentials at Baltimore recommended the admission of both delegations with power to each half of the vote of the State. The Convention did adopt this report but excluded the secession delegates and admitted the original delegation entirely. They however refused to take their seats in the Convention, except ten of the who did not secede from Charleston and who support National nominations of Douglas and Johnson.

Suffice me to add a few words from the extract of Mr. Johnson's speech of July 18 in the Senate which have been inserted in your book. It's remarkable to how exactly he took the position of the Supreme Court decision in the Dred Scott case long before such decision on the points, by the Supreme Court, was thought of. It shows that Mr. Johnson in the nation has an intellect capable of grasping and solving the most difficult questions of political science. He is one of the greatest statesmen of this country, any other or country.

Moreover Mr. Johnson is not and never was, a Disunionist, as he is frequently charged in Northern papers. I am well posted on this point and speak knowingly and correctly.

NATIVE GEORGIAN.
Warrington, D. C. Aug 11, 1850.


Remarks.

We gladly publish the foregoing and will correct future editions of the Text Book in conformity with the facts he points out. We make no objection to the writer's assertion that Mr. Johnson is an able man. As a man, we have no word to utter against him. But, as a politician, we have this to say, and we would call to it the attention of "A Native Georgian" from whom we shall gladly hear further:

1. He asserts that Mr. H. V. Johnson is not a Disunionist. This is no time for quibbling about words. Nobody imagines that Mr. Johnson or Mr. anybody else wants the Union dissolved so long as he and his set can rule it. But we do understand that Mr. H. V. Johnson has repeatedly declared that he could not submit to the government of the Union on Republican principles and by Republican men. Is this denied? If not, how is he any less Disunionist than Keitt, or Rhett, or Yancey?

2. Our correspondent insists that Mr. Johnson anticipated the decision of the Supreme Court in the Dred Scott case. Very likely. But did he then pretend to reconcile that decision with Popular Sovereignty? Can he not reconcile them? Here is the point on which the secession men seem to us to have immensely the advantage. They hold substantially the doctrines promulgated by Mr. Johnson, but they hold them consistently. They do not pretend, since the Dred Scott decision, that the people of a Territory, while it remains a Territory, can "CIRCULATE the Slavery question TO suit themselves." Douglas does pretend it, and, with impudence which Satan might envy, goes about from day to day asking "Why should not the people of a Territory, like those of a State, have Slavery or not have it as they see fit?"—when he knows perfectly well that the Cincinnati Platform, the Dred Scott Decision, and the Wickliffe plank in his platform, practically deny and preclude any right to exclude Slavery from Territory. So does Mr. Johnson's platform, reported to the Georgia Democratic Convention. Is not Mr. J. too much of a man to play part in this dishonest game of talking Popular Sovereignty and at the same time unfolding the Dred Scott decision?

3. Finally, we understand Mr. Johnson to maintain, in his Philadelphia Speech of 1856, that it is fittest and best that Capital should own Labor. We totally dissent from that suggestion, and cannot consider it indicative of a true statesman. Capital comes near enough to owning Labor under any social system yet fairly tried. We do not think true craftsmanship looks in that direction, but the opposite. What says "A Native Georgian"?

Just then one of the ladies remarked, "Oh, look, Mary, that feller with the white hat han't got his on the right place." Ditto thought we. Just then a ragged little devil sang out as he glided past us, "Hallo, old timber legs!" and we arose suddenly and put after him, and away went our legs—one to the east, the other to the west, causing a large, immense fissure in our pants, and another picture of a butter-tray in the cold—oh, hon, cold ice. Then the lady—we knew she was one by the remark she made—again she spoke and said, "Oh look, Mary, that chap with white hat has set down on his handkerchief to keep from taking cold!" We rose about as graceful as a horse, when Mary said, "Guess 'taint a handkerchief, Jane." And Mary was right. It wasn't a handkerchief, not a bit of it. Just then a friend came along, and proffered us his coat tail as a "steadler." But the ice is very cold, this season.

We tried it again. A glide one way—a glide and half the other, when whack came our bump of philoprogenitiveness on the ice, and we saw millions of stars dancing around us, like ballet girls at the Bowery Theater. How that shock went through our system, and up and down our spinal column. Light mining couldn't have corkscrewed it down a creased sapling with greater speed or more exhilarating effect. Boarding house butter nor warranty deed could not have struck stronger than we did—and dozen ladies looking at us—and our assured pants.

"Hallo, old cock!" sang out that ragged imp again, and we there helpless. Soon we got up and made another trial, with better success. Perhaps we had skated, in our peculiar style, fifteen feet, when a laundering chap came up behind, and we sat down with our tired head pillowed in his lap—and he swearing at us, when it was all his fault.

We have the great moral weight which the right always lends to any cause. Will secession amply and cowardly surrender of all the Territories to our Northern enemy? Is there the remedy for

The great interest about which we are so solicitous is that of slavery. Will secession render that interest more valuable? when we have secession, and thus deprived slave-labor of free northern markets; when we have destroyed the free interchange of produce between that species of labor and that of our Northern neighbors, which now adds so much to the profits of slavery—when we have imposed upon ourselves standing army and home-government and the taxes necessary to support them—when groaning under such burdensome taxation, we have become exhausted in treasury, in resources, in energy, and in spirit by civil war, will slavery be made more valuable? Will it not become rather a burden and a curse to those who own and have them to support? Worse than all, will not the thousands who do not own slaves naturally ask, why all this sacrifice? Will there not arise an abolition party in our very midst, and at our very firesides, thousand fold more formidable than the entire North, even if the entire North were abolitionists? Indeed, does not every statesman see that "secession" is the shortest possible road to abolition?

Let patriotism call upon them to wait. For two years at least. Mr. Lincoln's hands are tied. Before another four years shall have elapsed, his party will have disintegrated. The causes which gave rise to that party were all accidental. It had its origin in the repeal of the Missouri compromise. A desire to secure the admission of Kansas as a free State has fed it, and in the present election, attached to it a great conservative element at the North, which really had no affinity for it. The unfortunate division at Charleston, also gave it in this election all that horde of voters to be found everywhere, who have no settled principles, but who seek to get on the strong side. All these instrumentalities which have combined to give it its success, it is clear, are merely accidental, and before another election will have ceased to exist. The status of Kansas, as of all other of our Territories, will have become fixed. The South will, it is to be hoped, have become united and the Republican party, if it exist at all, will exist only in its naked sectional character, and hence drive off by law the larger portion of its present co-operators, who will then have no need of it as an instrumentality.

But it is said honor calls for secession? If that is true, let it come! As Union great and glorious destiny awaits us as Union, indeed, proud and pre-eminent place among nations is ours. With the riches of Europe and the West Indies pouring into our Eastern lap. With the wealth of the East ready to pour itself through our Pacific gate surrounded on all sides by Lakes and Gulf and Oceans, all ready to bear away the untold abundance of our soil traversed by the most majestic rivers of earth; with every species of soil, and every species of climate with an active, hardy and enterprising race of people; with internal development following close upon the heels of our fine and quickened internal trade, consequent upon our diversity of soil and climate, who cannot see that all our greatness is YET TO COME? Yet would I for one, be willing to see these splendid prospects, all, ALL, at one fell swoop, swept into utter annihilation, rather than submit to dishonor!

But is it true that "secession" is our only honorable course? Is it true that secession is honorable AT ALL? Let us fancy the picture. Let us suppose that instead of fighting for our rights in the Union we tamely abandon them. Let us suppose Southern Confederacy established, and what? A weakling government overburdened with its own enormous expenses and its standing army, instead of the first and greatest nation on the globe, as we now are; instead of that high title to sovereignty to which our industry, our intelligence and civilization entitle us, a mere, dwarfish, secondary power, occupying, as every one will see we will occupy, position of dependence—nay, of double dependence—independence upon our Northern neighbors for protection against European aggression, dependence upon European assistance for protection against northern aggression. What man who has the pride of the patriotism of a true American, but recoils from the dishonoring spectacle—May God in his mercy avert the humiliation—is the prayer of yours, truly.

W. W. FISHBACK.

GREENWOOD, ARK, Dec 31ST, 1860.

AS SEEN AT ANTIOCH COLLEGE, YELLOW SPRINGS.

Mr. J. A. Preston of Yellow Springs witnessed the meteor under very favorable circumstances for observation. He gives us the following description:

Between nineteen and twenty minutes past ten o'clock of the evening, while sitting with one of the students there, appeared in the sky a bright ball resembling the sun in red color, which was recognized as a meteor and collected my observations. It passed for 10 seconds increasing in branacy from pale red to very white, encircled by rings of light, then shot through the heavens in a horizontal wavering line from east to west with immense velocity. At first sparks of fire were emitted, which charged the fiery ball. Increased red streams of light of the beautiful colors and of such intensity as to dazzle the eyes and left in its very large luminous trail a circle of diameter in which several colors of the rainbow were distinctly visible. It passed but one ball. As it entered the western horizon it was more irregular and the flame again changed to deep crimson ball, continuing its antics behind the clouds leaving a trace of us pale on it. During few seconds of its existence the radiance of the southern heavens perfectly presented a grand pyrotechnic display in which the ball was the centerpiece. During this PHENOMENON the stars were wholly obscured by heavy cloud which rendered the spectacle more brilliant. The duration of the display, I do think, was 10 to 15 seconds. There was a report but faint hiss in the air produced by the conclusion of air distinctly heard, and I do not know why there is mention of it in the Cincinnati papers of yesterday morning of short duration and less in its magnitude than that the light was certainly as brilliant and wonderful.

a horse some three weeks previous. DR. Arm-
strong was an early missionary to the Sandwich
Islands. He was born at McEvansville, Pa, April
13, 1805, graduated at Dickinson College, and stud-
ied for the ministry at Princeton Seminary. He
went to Honolulu in 1832, and after laboring as a
missionary for number of years, taken into
the King's service. He won high reputation, and
was much esteemed by both native and foreign
residents.


UNION MEETING IN NEW YORK.—The Young Mem-
bers Union Club, of New York, met at their headquar-
ters, Broadway, on Wednesday evening. It was ex-
pected that the Hon. Mr. Hilliard, of Alabama,
would address them on the great issue of the day.
The gentlemen, however, was prevented by press-
ing business from attending. The meeting was ad-
dressed by ex-Mayor Swift of this city, who
entered into the questions affecting the Union
and recommended coalition of the conservative
men of the country for the preservation of our COM-
mon rights.


From NICARAGUA.—By late advices from Ni-
caragua learn that President Martinez, of
Nicaragua, in a proclamation thanking the people
for their patriotic efforts during the recent lib-
eration excitements, urges the necessity of the
five republics of Central America becoming consolidated,
for their greater strength and security, under the
title of the Republic of Central America, and offers
for his part, to lay down all his authority at the
feet of a central government.


COTTON COMING OVER THE VIRGINIA ROUTE.—The
Bristol (Va.) News, of Friday, says:
"Some forty carloads of cotton, comprising
1880 bales arrived at the Tennessee depot in this
place, the past week, and are detained here in con-
sequence of the break in the Virginia and Tennessee
Railroad. This is the first shipment of the season
from Memphis to Norfolk, and is but earnest of
the immense amount of cotton which will probably
seek transportation over this route."


GOING SOUTH.—The number of young men who have
left Quebec during the last few days for the south
States according to the Chronicle, is positively
astonishing, and surpasses by far the number of
those who were in the habit of seeking their for-
tunes in the South during the winter of former
years. The figure will scarcely fall short of six
hundred. They nearly all belong to the working
classes connected with the shipping, and bound
for Savannah, New Orleans, Mobile, Pensacola and
other southern ports.


THREE CARLOADS of provisions arrived at Atchi-
son, Kansas, on Monday, for the relief of the set-
tlers of the territory, making six carloads within
the past week, and each carload ranging from six
to eight tons. Teams waiting to be loaded
from Greenwood, Butler, Breckenridge and Otto
counties. Supplies given to those only who
have proper credentials from the neighborhood
from which they come, and are duly authorized by
the Relief Committee to receive them.


PAID FIRE DEPARTMENT IN RICHMOND.—CITY
Councils of Richmond, Va, have passed bill to
reorganize the fire department upon the paid sys-
TEM, and to employ limited number of steam
engines in connection with the hand machines.
The department is to consist of 1 principal engi-
neer, four commanders, four foremen, and seventy
two firemen; also, one engineer, one fireman, and
one hustler, with one steam fire engine, three hand
engines, one hook and ladder truck, reels, hose,
and other apparatus attached.


COMPRESSED IRON.—We understand, says the Phil-
adelphia Ledger, that some interesting experiments
have been made by Merrick Sons, in this city, as
to the strength of iron compressed by cold rolling.

gave a strength of about 110,900 pounds per square
inch for iron, which, before being thus rolled, bore
but about 65,900 pounds. Iron thus rolled is being
used BY another firm in making divided axles for
city railroad cars.

Fortunately it has been discovered not in time to prevent the destruction by fire of half a million of property, but in time to save the lives of the people, and it is hoped to bring the ringleaders, particularly the hellish inciters of the negroes, to justice.

FURTHER PARTICULARS IN Cruyer.

Mr. Cruyer, just down from Upper Waxahachie, confirms his accounts we say received from Dr. Py. H. says his vigilance committee consists of the best men in the Texas counties; that they are acting with great caution and deliberativeness, and that the people have the utmost confidence in them. He also states that in Dallas they have some eight or ten negroes, who applied to see the ring leaders in confidence. They will probably be hung. Mr. Cruyer had witnessed some seventy or eighty who knew of the conspiracies, but failed to inform on the conspirators. In Waxahachie, the discovery was made through the voluntary confession of one negro, bringing to N. Waxahachie, Texas, the names of several enablers, i.e., H. Tarrant, and Benson, and the testimony of the negroes has been the same. They have all agreed in every respect that they were to burn the houses and murder women on the first Monday, and also they were then to attack the people. The plan was to reinforce with men expected from Liberia band, and having got possession of arms, provision, and fight their way to Mexico.

We met Mr. Cruyer two weeks since. Waxahachie, this Monday, there was rum that there had been two men hung in Dallas, and he thinks those must be the men alluded to in the letters from Chi. The people in six parts of the county are thoroughly stirred, and will not stop until the whole plot is laid bare and the offenders so far as possible, are brought to justice.

We hear reports from Grimes, but they want confirmation, and we will not report them. The people say, however, every sort of the stir and suspicious characters are being strictly watched.

SANGAMON.


Garibaldi's Expedition.--Critical Position of Affairs in Europe.


This great revolutionary leader is again attracting the attention of the world, being at present engaged in the most hazardous of his Enterprises, a life or death struggle with the Neapolitan Government. The late intelligence from Europe informs us that he landed at Marsala, in Sicily, with about 1000 followers, and was immediately attacked by the royal troops. It is said that one of his steamers has been sunk and the other captured; but if he succeeded in landing his artillery and ammunition, it is probable that the loss of his transports will not interfere with his operations. As he has made no arrangements for retreat, his motto is "Onward, to death or glory." Garibaldi possesses much sagacity, and it is not likely that he undertook this desperate enterprise without ascertaining the sentiments of Victor Emanuel and Napoleon III, and as both these sovereigns favor the expulsion of the Bourbons from the throne of Naples and the annexation of that Kingdom to the Italian Confederation, it is possible that they may have encouraged the present expedition. It is certain that there cannot be true freedom in Italy while one of the infamous Bourbons wields a sceptre, or controls dungeon, on that Peninsula, and if the patriots are successful in the Island of Sicily, the Straits of Messina are too narrow to prevent the flame of Liberty from reaching the mainland.


The marriage of the cousin of the Emperor of the French to the daughter of the King of Sardinia foreshadowed coming events, for this alliance indicated that the old Napoleonic policy of attaching all Italy to the interests of France was not abandoned. If the expedition in support of Garibaldi is permitted to join him, the power of the King of Naples will be overthrown, unless events occur for which the public is totally unprepared. Russia is favorable to the present dynasty of Naples, because the late King Ferdinand refused supplies of corn to the Allies during the Crimean War, and Alexander II may lend his aid in the hour of need to put down revolution in the Neapolitan dominions, especially as by doing so, he would be thwarting the designs of Victor Emanuel. However this may be, it is certain that Russia is collecting large numbers of transports at Nicholaef, Crimean port, which, since the dismantling of Sevastopol, is her principal naval station in the Black Sea and its tributaries. It may be said that Russia is bound by treaty not to enlarge her fleet, and that the guns of the Dardanelles are MORALLY pointed against her. This is true, but the most solemn treaties have been violated by the Emperor of France, and this is good precedent for the Czar of Russia to NEEDLE in the affairs of Turkey or Naples. Great events are looming in the distance. We will watch their development with anxiety.

USED FOR FRAUD.—The United States Attorney-Gen-
eral has given opinion sustaining the action of the
Postmaster, of Baltimore who refused to deliver let-
ters addressed to fictitious persons or firms. The
Attorney-General says the postmaster has authori-
ty under the laws to prevent the service from being
used for fraudulent purposes, and then adds:

With that end IN view, you certainly have power
to order the non-delivery of letters addressed to any
person under a name which you know to have
been assumed, part of system intended to cheat
and defraud the public. But the fraudulent intent
ought to be very clear for you are not invested with
any authority to carry an extended inquiry into
private affairs of persons who receive letters by
mail nor have you the means of ascertaining with
correctness what they are. It should also be re-
membered that the mere misnomer of a man is not
sufficient grounds for saying that the name is fic-
titious neither is the firm imaginary one because
the style of it has no reference to the ofits
members. Nor can you stop a letter the sole
ground that it is addressed to a person whose en-
deavour is immoral it being the duty of the State
government and not of the Post Office Department to
punish such offenses. But if in the under con-
sideration if there be legitimate business of any
kind carried by C., under the name of D. & Co.,
and he has caused letters be addressed to Baltimore
in a name which is merely imaginary, if his cor-
RESPONDENTS do not know whom they are writing
to—and if in addition to this you find the fact that
C. is using this fiction for dishonest purposes, then
the measures taken by the postmaster at Baltimore
ought to be sustained.

It is a remarkable and very instructive fact
that many of the most important operations of
nature are carried on in unbroken silence. —
There is no rushing sound when the broad tide
of sunlight breaks on a dark world and floods
it with glory, as one bright wave after another
falls from the fountain, millions of miles away.
There is no cracking of heavy axes or groaning
of cumbersome machinery as the solid earth
wheels on its way, and every planet and system
performs its revolutions. The great trees bring
forth their bounty and shadow the earth be-
neath them—the plants cover themselves with
buds, and the buds burst into flowers; but the
whole transaction is unheard. The change,
from snow and winter winds to the blossoms
and fruits and sunshine of summer, is seen in
its slow development, but there is scarcely a
sound to tell of the mighty transformation.
The solemn chant of the ocean, as it raises its
unchanged and unceasing voice, the roar of
the hurricane, and the soft notes of the breeze,
the rushing of the mountain river, and the
thunder of the black-browed storm; all this is
the music of nature—a great and swelling al-
lem of praise, breaking in on the universal
calm. There is a lesson for us here. The
mightiest worker in the universe is the most
unobtrusive.
